Region Comparison Network is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and is reported to outperform existing baselines while adding region-level interpretability through Region Activation Mapping. Its experimental dimension is therefore different from a pure embedding-loss paper: the comparison tests whether learned query–support region correspondence improves and explains decisions, not only whether latent classes are more compact. Because the excerpt gives no exact accuracies, backbone table, or confidence estimates, the supported statement is that RCN demonstrated effectiveness over its selected baselines on the four cited benchmarks under its own protocol. It can be compared mechanistically with global Relation Networks—RCN adds spatially localized correspondence—but not numerically ranked from the supplied text alone. RankDNN is evaluated as a learnable ranking head on miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, CUB, and CIFAR-FS, and the paper reports that it improves a variety of backbone baselines and outperforms previous algorithms; its cross-domain experiments also indicate stronger transferability in the authors' setup. This makes the evidence backbone-conditional in an important sense: RankDNN can be placed on top of different feature extractors and fused with post-processing, so an observed gain reflects the ranking module together with the chosen extractor and fusion setting. Without the exact per-backbone numbers, it is not valid to claim that its MLP comparator beats RCN, SRL, or prototype methods under a common backbone. [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58]

MSENet tests the value of multi-stage features in 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot episodes on MiniImageNet and FC100, followed by cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets. Its comparison targets the limitation of using a single distance over final-layer features: stage-wise outputs, self-attention refinement, and learnable stage weights are evaluated as a combined representation-and-fusion method. The excerpt reports high cross-domain accuracy and efficacy relative to state-of-the-art approaches, but it does not provide the exact percentages or matched model sizes in the selected text. Consequently, MSENet can be said to broaden the comparison from one embedding space to multiple weighted feature spaces, but its numerical advantage cannot be reconstructed or directly compared here. [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:e9dd9ee8e005]

The Siamese Transformer Network is evaluated on four popular few-shot benchmarks in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings and reports superior performance to the state-of-the-art baselines included in its study. Its experimental contribution is a controlled architectural combination in the paper's framework: self-supervised ViT-Small initialization, separate global and local branches, Euclidean distance for global features, KL divergence for local features, L2 normalization, and weighted fusion. Since the excerpt omits exact scores and does not establish that the same pretraining is supplied to all competitors, the result should be interpreted as evidence for global/local fusion under that transformer setup rather than as proof that two distances always outperform single-distance metric learning. [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45]

Cross-domain tests form a separate comparison axis. Deep K-tuplet trains on miniImageNet and evaluates on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars, and the paper reports that it significantly outperforms prior methods in that cross-dataset setting. Proto-Triplet and ICNN also test CUB, Caltech, Dogs, and Cars and report competitive generalization, while MSENet reports tests across eight target datasets and RankDNN reports a cross-domain challenge. These studies all concern transfer away from the source benchmark, but their target versions, backbones, source-training assumptions, and exact metrics are not shown to be identical in the excerpts. They therefore support a qualitative pattern—embedding geometry, ranking, and multi-stage features can be designed with transfer in mind—but not a cross-paper winner. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:cfe8011f36d7] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:508afe07fba7] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:c9a16c8b4307] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:83140db1cc86] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:4:fc29f7338649:claim:982b41a3ea6f] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:e9dd9ee8e005] [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58]

Supervision and adaptation assumptions create another non-comparable dimension. ProtoTransfer is compared with unsupervised meta-learning on miniImageNet and is reported to outperform those methods; under domain shift it is reported to be comparable to supervised methods while requiring orders of magnitude fewer labels. That result answers a label-efficiency question, not the same question as a fully supervised K-tuplet or relation-network comparison. Likewise, transductive cross-entropy fine-tuning is reported to outperform current state-of-the-art methods on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 using the same hyperparameters, but it is a strong transfer/fine-tuning baseline rather than a metric learner. Its reported success challenges benchmark interpretation but cannot be read as a metric-method result unless prediction and adaptation settings are matched. [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:124d7f0c2b82] [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:097e69f218ad] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:417553186fa2]

Domain-specific sensor benchmarks require their own tables. In FewSAR, 15 classic few-shot methods are implemented in three categories and evaluated under unified SAR protocols with both quantitative results and runtime; the benchmark authors observe that metric-learning methods attain the best accuracy, whereas meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, which they attribute primarily to bias in existing datasets. This is direct evidence only for the SAR benchmark and its included methods. The hyperspectral multi-level relation method similarly reports gains over state-of-the-art cross-domain hyperspectral approaches by combining contrastive class-level relations and transformer cross-attention with a domain discriminator. Neither SAR nor hyperspectral accuracy should be compared numerically with natural-image miniImageNet scores because sensor bands, class structure, domain shift, and protocol implementation differ. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:30ce48d809b4] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b]

Across matched evidence, the practical experimental picture is therefore multidimensional. Simple nearest-support and prototype methods provide low-complexity reference decisions; learned relation, region, and ranking heads improve comparison flexibility when trained episodically; K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and ICNN directly target embedding geometry; SRL and subspace models trade a richer class model for support-diversity requirements; MSENet and STN purchase multi-level or global/local information with more architecture and pretraining; and ProtoTransfer changes the label-budget question. The only numerical head-to-head values available in the selected excerpts are the Proto-Triplet/ICNN Mini-ImageNet scores. Other superiority claims are source-supported but remain conditional on each paper's baselines and protocol, so they indicate where evidence exists without supporting an overall ranking. Limitations and Open Problems

A central few-shot risk is that the support set contains only one or a few labeled examples. Direct nearest-support methods classify from those individual support samples, while prototypes summarize scarce support evidence into a point and can compress within-class variation into that reference. Distributional or subspace representations are intended to capture class variation, and the review reports the Deep Subspace Network line as more robust than Prototypical Networks to noise and outliers; nevertheless, those richer models still estimate their class representation from the same scarce support set. The selected sources therefore support scarcity as a basic challenge, but do not establish a general failure condition for every embedding, subspace, or relation score. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:19a19b550bc8] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:3194b68af4ef] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:109e350ee013] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:417553186fa2]

Embedding-space constraints introduce a sampling and mining trade-off. Deep K-tuplet explicitly addresses the limitation of an ordinary triplet update seeing only one negative by jointly comparing K negatives and using semi-hard mining to select informative hard triplets; the paper presents this as a way to speed convergence and stabilize training. Proto-Triplet and ICNN similarly enforce intra-class compactness and inter-class separation, with ICNN using batch-level nearest-neighbor distances, variance, and class-ratio statistics. The cited papers support the need for informative triplets or batch statistics, but they do not establish that particular failure modes such as too-easy negatives, overly hard negatives, batch imbalance, or universally unstable training occur in these methods. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:cfe8011f36d7] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:508afe07fba7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:83140db1cc86] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:4:fc29f7338649:claim:982b41a3ea6f] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:10e3a8ec7066]

Learned comparators add learned modules to the decision stage. Relation Networks learn a nonlinear relation score instead of using a fixed cosine or Euclidean metric, RCN learns region-level query–support comparisons, and RankDNN uses an MLP ranking head that can be placed on different feature extractors and fused with post-processing. RCN's source-supported design is specifically directed toward corresponding regions and interpretability through Region Activation Mapping. RankDNN's reported gains are conditional on the backbone and fusion with which the ranking head is deployed. The selected sources do not establish a general overfitting or vulnerability claim for every flexible comparator under changed support statistics, image style, or target domain. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a195d65d3a29] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:c8bbee298669] [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:16194f2dc624] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:fef0a0efd75f]

Representation-rich designs carry architectural and pretraining dependencies. MSENet addresses the shallow-feature limitation of a single final-layer distance by using multiple stage outputs, self-attention refinement, and learnable stage weights; STN combines self-supervised ViT-Small global and local branches with Euclidean distance, KL divergence, normalization, and weighted fusion. Because the cited results evaluate these components as packaged systems, they do not isolate a universal rule that adding more features always helps. Their use also depends on access to the stated multi-output or transformer architecture and the reported self-supervised initialization; the selected text does not provide a separate compute-cost analysis. [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:e9dd9ee8e005] [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45]

Cross-domain generalization is a separate evaluation axis. Deep K-tuplet trains on miniImageNet and tests Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars; Proto-Triplet/ICNN also test CUB, Caltech, Dogs, and Cars; RankDNN reports a cross-domain challenge; and MSENet reports tests across eight benchmark datasets. These results support transfer claims only within each paper's source and target protocol. The selected excerpts do not show that source training sets, target versions, backbones, or supervision assumptions are matched across these papers. They therefore do not support cross-paper numerical rankings or a claim that any one model is domain invariant. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:cfe8011f36d7] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:c9a16c8b4307] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:83140db1cc86] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:4:fc29f7338649:claim:982b41a3ea6f] [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:e9dd9ee8e005]

Domain-specific sensor imagery requires separate evaluation. Under FewSAR's unified SAR protocols, the benchmark reports that metric-learning methods attain the best accuracy while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, with the authors attributing that pattern primarily to bias in existing datasets. The cross-domain hyperspectral method instead combines a domain discriminator, contrastive class-level relations, and transformer cross-attention for source–target mismatch. These findings support treating SAR and hyperspectral settings as distinct from natural-image benchmarks; the selected sources do not justify a general claim that every natural-image metric design is unsuitable for either sensor domain. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:30ce48d809b4] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b]

Supervision assumptions change the comparison. ProtoTransfer uses unlabeled prototypical samples and augmentations to construct a self-supervised metric embedding, then summarizes class clusters and fine-tunes; it is reported to outperform state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on miniImageNet and to be comparable to supervised methods under domain shift while using orders of magnitude fewer labels. That evidence addresses a label-budget setting and does not establish parity under identical supervision with fully supervised episodic metric learners. The transductive cross-entropy fine-tuning study reports strong results on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 and explicitly motivates stronger scrutiny of current benchmarks and protocols, making it an important matched baseline rather than a metric-learning method. [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:124d7f0c2b82] [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:097e69f218ad] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:417553186fa2]

Benchmark and episode heterogeneity limits cross-paper ordering. The selected studies report common datasets and 5-way 1-shot or 5-way 5-shot settings, but the excerpts do not provide a common backbone, training schedule, augmentation, transductiveness setting, episode count, confidence interval, or runtime across all methods. Proto-Triplet and ICNN can be compared numerically within their own paper, and FewSAR explicitly reports quantitative results and runtime under its unified SAR setting. Other superiority claims remain tied to each paper's selected baselines and protocols. The fine-tuning study also proposes an episode-hardness metric, indicating that average accuracy alone may not fully characterize task difficulty. [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:4:fc29f7338649:claim:982b41a3ea6f] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:30ce48d809b4] [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:097e69f218ad] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:8f2d3aeed0e0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062]

Interpretability is most explicit in RCN among the approaches discussed here. RCN learns region-level comparisons and provides Region Activation Mapping plus category-level prototypical-part explanations, making some query–support evidence inspectable. The other decision rules discussed in the selected sources expose less direct visual evidence: a nearest prototype gives a distance-based class choice, while learned relation scores, weighted stage fusion, global/local weighting, or cross-attention are not accompanied in the excerpts by validated faithful-explanation evidence. Thus, interpretability should be evaluated separately from accuracy rather than assumed from a learned score or attention-like component. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a195d65d3a29] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:c8bbee298669] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0] [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b]

The cited methods expose different trade-offs rather than a universal winner. Nearest-support and prototype comparisons use simple class representations; embedding losses such as K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and ICNN add geometry constraints and sampling requirements; subspace and distributional representations attempt to model variation; relation, region, ranking, multi-stage, and transformer methods add learned modules or pretraining dependencies; and ProtoTransfer changes the supervision and label-budget setting. Because the available evidence comes from different datasets, shot settings, backbones, supervision assumptions, and domains, method choice should be evaluated on the target protocol rather than inferred from unmatched benchmark averages. The selected excerpts do not support a universal computational-cost ranking across all methods. Conclusion

For a target few-shot image task, the defensible choice is not a single universally dominant metric learner. Nearest-support and prototype approaches are low-complexity baselines when the learned embedding is reliable; embedding losses are appropriate when latent geometry is the main bottleneck and informative batches or mining are available; subspace or distributional representations target within-class variation but depend on support diversity; learned relation, region, ranking, multi-stage and global/local comparators can exploit nonlinear, spatial or hierarchical evidence at the cost of added modules, training dependence or pretraining. RCN additionally supplies region-based visual explanation, whereas the other comparators discussed do not have matched faithful-explanation evidence in the excerpts. claim_records.text: The proposed deep K-tuplet network extends the classical triplet network from deep metric learning for few-shot learning, utilizing relationships among input samples to learn general representations via episode-training.

The trained deep K-tuplet network can extract discriminative features for unseen novel categories and can be seamlessly incorporated with a non-linear distance metric function to facilitate few-shot classification.
The proposed method's result on the miniImageNet benchmark outperforms other metric-based few-shot classification methods.

When evaluated on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars using the model trained with miniImageNet, the proposed method significantly outperforms prior methods, demonstrating superior capability to generalize to unseen classes.

The deep K-tuplet Network generalizes the triplet network to allow joint comparison with K negative samples in each mini-batch, making feature embedding learning more faithful to few-shot classification with improved feature generalization.
The semi-hard mining sampling technique is presented as an effective sampling strategy to sample informative hard triplets, which can speed up convergence and stabilize the training procedure.
The proposed technique can be seamlessly incorporated with the learnable non-linear distance metric for few-shot classification.

fact_fields.method: deep K-tuplet Network with semi-hard mining sampling

claim_records.text: The proposed method outperforms other metric-based methods and achieves competitive performance over other meta-based methods on the miniImageNet benchmark.

A new experimental setting is established for evaluating the cross-domain generalization ability of few-shot classification algorithms, and the proposed method's results generalized on CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars and Caltech-101 excel other methods, showing excellent cross-domain generalization capacity.

The proposed method performs target tasks based entirely on feed-forward without requiring further parameter updates, unlike meta-learner based methods that need to fine-tune or update parameters for new unseen tasks.
The prototypical network builds a pre-class prototype representation for few-shot classification.
The relation network learns a nonlinear distance metric via a shallow neural network instead of using a fixed linear distance metric such as Cosine and Euclidean.
Naively fine-tuning a model on novel labeled data would easily over-fit the few given data, so data augmentation and regularization are often employed to relieve the overfitting.

claim_records.text: The proposed Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The proposed ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The proposed loss functions show a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed methods demonstrate competitive generalization capabilities to other domains including Caltech, CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets compared with the state of the art.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The obtained accuracy results on Mini-Imagenet represent an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The ICNN Loss measures the intra and inter class distances of batch points and assigns each data point an Inter and Intra Class Nearest Neighbors score.
The Proto-Triplet Loss is based on triplet loss and calculates the similarity between points using prototypes of different classes as anchor, positive, and negative points.
Both the ICNN Loss and Proto-Triplet Loss aim to increase the inter-class distance and decrease the intra-class distance between samples of different classes.
The ICNN loss represents a novel loss function that evaluates the quality of the features obtained based on the inter/intra class, the variance and the class ratio from nearest neighbors.
Current deep learning algorithms tend to overfit when they are given a small dataset for training, limiting their generalization capabilities.

The main challenge for few-shot learning is to apply a fine-tuning process to an existing embedding network to adapt it to new classes, and such process can easily lead to overfitting due to the few labeled samples available for each class.
Metric-learning methods learn a pairwise similarity metric such that a score given by some distance is high for similar samples, whilst dissimilar samples get a low score.
Only a few methods have explored mechanisms for enforcing class separability via a custom loss function during training.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification classify unseen samples by their distances to few seen samples in a learned deep neural network embedding space, avoiding overfitting to few training images and achieving state-of-the-art performance.

This review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification published from 2018 to 2022 into three groups aligned with three metric learning stages: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of novel classes are classified by computing their distances to novel support images under the learned measure, followed by a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest neighbors.

fact_fields.method: Supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify query samples by measuring and comparing their distance to support samples, but scarce support samples have limited capacity to represent the novel class.

Class prototypes used in few-shot metric learning can be constructed as simple or weighted averages of feature embeddings, or learned end-to-end to improve representation ability; some works also use class distributions or subspaces as class representations.

Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure sample distances, and computes query class assignment confidence by estimating each class distribution via a neural network.

fact_fields.method: Variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning

claim_records.text: Simon et al. proposed the Deep Subspace Network (DSN), which represents each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition, and classifies queries by nearest subspace assignment based on Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class subspace.
The DSN method is reported to be more robust to noises and outliers than the Prototypical Network.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-support pair similarities and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.
UAFS converts observed query-support similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporates them into the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to jointly consider similarities between a query and prototypes in a support set and estimate the uncertainty of each query-prototype pair.

fact_fields.method: Graph-based model for similarity uncertainty estimation

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments show the proposed UAFS method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, UAFS takes each query-prototype pair as a node and employs a graph-based model to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each pair.

Rather than a scalar, UAFS models the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj by a distribution, referred to as probabilistic similarity, based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation.

fact_fields.method: Probabilistic similarity modeling with graph-based uncertainty estimation

claim_records.text: The UAFS network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses that exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.

fact_fields.method: Uncertainty-aware optimization with similarity-based classification losses

claim_records.text: Few-shot image classification aims to classify query samples of new categories given only a few labeled support samples of these categories.

In similarity-based few-shot classification, the logit vector for a query sample is obtained by feeding similarities between the query and prototypes to a SoftMax function, making the reliability of estimated similarity vital to classification performance.
Aleatoric uncertainty captures noise inherent in observations and identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample.
For few-shot image classification, an observed query-prototype similarity suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.

In the proposed UAFS framework, the observed feature similarity between a query and a prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

Experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models and provides consistent improvements on few-shot classification performance under domain shift.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method proposed for few-shot image classification that aims to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify specific mutually related regions in query and support images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
RCN's interpretability can be generalized from the task level to the category level, which can be viewed as a way to find prototypical parts supporting RCN's final decision.
Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets show RCN is effective over existing baselines for few-shot image classification.
RCN's final classification decision is directly linked to region similarities in the last layer, forming a simple and easily explained linear process compared to attention mechanisms.
RCN includes a region meta learner, a dynamic system designed to adapt to different meta tasks during both training and testing stages.
RCN learns a generated weight of regions to explain which regions in a support sample are similar to locations in a query sample and which of these regions the model prefers to compare.
RCN is designed to find which parts in a query sample are most similar to manually selected regions in a support sample by computing similarity between them.
RCN generates a region weight in its final stage to define which common parts between support and query samples most influence the final similarity score.
Few-shot learning methods are grouped into metric-based models and gradient-based models in the presented related work review.

claim_records.text: MF-Adapter (Meta-Feature Adaption method) combines complementary strengths of low-level local representations and high-level semantic representations for few-shot classification.
MF-Unit (Meta-Feature Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric designed to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.

MF-Unit is obtained by inductive representation of local feature maps at different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information representing category-consistent characteristics.

Before model training, support set images are encoded into different-level features by a fixed CLIP visual encoder, and low-level feature maps are unfolded into Meta-Feature using a list of sliding windows with different scales.
MF-Unit is calculated by applying inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window, and is regarded as category-consistent features containing inductive knowledge.

During inference, MF-Adapter first converts test images into MF-Units at different levels and scales, retrieves few-shot knowledge in the support set's MF-Unit space to get local logits, then combines this with the original CLIP high-level prediction for the final prediction.
MF-Adapter is the first work to utilize the local similarity of CLIP for few-shot learning, combining complementary strengths of low-level and high-level semantic representations.
Comprehensive experiments on 11 widely adopted datasets for few-shot classification show MF-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with previous CLIP-based methods.
Existing CLIP-based few-shot methods including CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features fully aligned with textual features representing the 'Summary' of images.
Low-level local representations (LRs) are more consistent between seen and unseen samples than high-level representations for few-shot classification.

In few-shot classification with insufficient seen images, the standard 'pre-training & fine-tuning' paradigm does not produce better results, so common practice is to fix CLIP pre-training weights and learn a lightweight module.
Tip-Adapter achieves large performance gains compared to both prompt-based methods and CLIP-Adapter on several classification datasets by fine-tuning a trainable query-key cache layer on top of CLIP.

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks are proposed for few-shot classification, where a classifier must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set given only a small number of examples of each new class.
Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classification is performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class.
Prototypical networks reflect a simpler inductive bias beneficial in the limited-data few-shot regime and achieve excellent results compared to recent few-shot learning approaches.
Analysis shows that some simple design decisions for prototypical networks can yield substantial improvements over recent approaches involving complicated architectural choices and meta-learning.
Prototypical networks extended to zero-shot learning achieve state-of-the-art results on the CU-Birds dataset.

claim_records.text: The subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image by exploiting a subspace in local CNN feature space, and measures similarity between two images according to a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).

claim_records.text: The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, compared to most previous works that adopted global vector representation.
Experimental results on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) demonstrate competitive/superior performance of the SRL framework compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

claim_records.text: Some recent work shows that local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.

Existing local descriptor based few-shot learning works are still based on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure relations between query images and support classes.
Given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class, an asymmetric measure is argued to be more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning.
The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes as input an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: The proposed QSFormer model integrates a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch to simultaneously model the two core challenges of few-shot classification.

The sampleFormer branch of QSFormer adopts Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model Support representation, Query image representation and metric learning for few-shot classification.

The local patch Transformer branch of QSFormer extracts structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches, serving as a complement to the global learning branch.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the QSFormer few-shot learning method.
All modules of QSFormer are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, thereby overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks with the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
The STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
The STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During training, the STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.

Extensive experiments show the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: Network intrusion detection systems face significant challenges in identifying emerging attack patterns, especially when limited data samples are available.

The proposed Multi-Space Prototypical Learning (MSPL) framework operates across multiple metric spaces—Euclidean, Cosine, Chebyshev, and Wasserstein distances—integrated through a constrained weighting scheme to enhance embedding robustness and improve pattern recognition.
The MSPL framework leverages Polyak-averaged prototype generation to stabilize the learning process and effectively adapt to rare and zero-day attacks.
The MSPL framework uses an episodic training paradigm to ensure balanced representation across diverse attack classes, enabling robust generalization.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) obtains the relational map between supports and queries effectively for few-shot tasks.

FS-CT consists of two parts: a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.

Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, enhances the transformer module significantly and improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
FS-CT performs competitive results in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition is developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.
FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm that can be applied for a wide range of applications, such as healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed for cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two core steps: 1) Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and 2) Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The RMP step of HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, to support better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

The REP step of HelixFormer uses CSRMs to strengthen extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.
Experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks show HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The official code for HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics under low-data regimes.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless for classification due to limited receptive field.

DMN4 (Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network) is proposed for FSL, which establishes a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation to explicitly select query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters.

fact_fields.method: DMN4 (Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network)

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMN4 outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both fine-grained and generalized datasets.

Extensive experiments carried on inductive FSL tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the COSOC approach.

FiT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the VTAB-1k benchmark using fewer than 1% of the updateable parameters.

FiT demonstrates parameter efficiency and superior accuracy in distributed low-shot applications including model personalization and federated learning where model update size is an important performance metric.
The parameter efficiency of FiT enables few-shot learning, inexpensive model updates for personalization, and communication efficient federated learning.

claim_records.text: In meta-learning for few-shot classification, the number of labeled examples per category used during meta-training impacts recognition performance at meta-test time.
Generally, the shot number used in meta-training should match the shot number used in meta-testing to obtain the best few-shot classification performance.
The paper introduces a theoretical analysis of the impact of shot number on Prototypical Networks, a state-of-the-art few-shot classification method.
The paper proposes a simple method that is robust to the choice of shot number used during meta-training, a crucial hyperparameter for few-shot learning.

claim_records.text: The model trained for an arbitrary meta-training shot number shows strong performance across different values of meta-testing shot numbers.
The proposed approach is experimentally demonstrated on different few-shot classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: The introduced semi-supervised few-shot learning approach, Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN), is built on top of Prototypical Networks (PN).
The developed random walk semi-supervised loss enables the network to learn representations that are compact and well-separated.

Compact and well-separated class representations can be achieved by modeling the prototypical random walk notion without needing additional graph-NN parameters or a transductive setting where a collective test set is provided.
The PRWN model outperforms baselines in most benchmarks, with significant improvements in some cases.
PRWN trained with 40% of data as labeled compares competitively against fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% of labels.

fact_fields.method: Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN) vs fully supervised Prototypical Networks

claim_records.text: In the 1-shot mini-Imagenet case, PRWN trained with 40% labeled data achieves 50.89% accuracy, outperforming fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% labels which achieve 49.4% accuracy.

claim_records.text: The PRWN loss is resistant to distractors, unlabeled data that does not belong to any of the training classes, reflecting robustness to labeled/unlabeled class distribution mismatch.

claim_records.text: Boundary patches corresponding to pixels located at the boundary of objects in hyperspectral images are hard to classify, as they are mixed with multi-class spectral information.
The proposed APNT method uses a transformer as feature extractor to learn pixel-to-pixel relations and apply different attentions to different pixels, with the prototype network as the backbone.

APNT randomly mixes up two hyperspectral image patches to imitate boundary patches, using these synthetic patches for training to enlarge the number of hard training samples and enhance their diversity.
APNT follows the TransMix data augmentation technique, using attention returned by the transformer to mix up labels of two patches to generate better labels for synthetic patches.
The proposed APNT method demonstrates state of the art performance and better robustness for few-shot hyperspectral image classification compared with existing methods in experiments.

Few-shot hyperspectral image classification aims to identify the class of each pixel using only a small number of labeled pixels, and fixed-size patches centered around each pixel are commonly used to obtain spatial-spectral joint features.
APNT does not directly use patches cut from hyperspectral images for training, instead using randomly mixed synthetic patches.

claim_records.text: Proto-CLIP is a few-shot learning framework that leverages large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP, utilizing both image prototypes and text prototypes for few-shot learning.

Proto-CLIP adapts image and text encoder embeddings from CLIP in a joint fashion using few-shot examples, and uses embeddings from the two encoders to compute respective image class prototypes for classification.

During adaptation, Proto-CLIP aligns image and text prototypes of corresponding classes, and this alignment is beneficial for few-shot classification due to reinforced contributions from both types of prototypes.
Proto-CLIP has both training-free and fine-tuned variants.
The effectiveness of Proto-CLIP is demonstrated via experiments on benchmark datasets for few-shot learning, as well as in real-world robot perception scenarios.
Proto-CLIP is motivated by unimodal prototypical networks for few-shot learning.

claim_records.text: The proposed deep K-tuplet network extends the classical triplet network from deep metric learning for few-shot learning, utilizing relationships among input samples to learn general representations via episode-training.

The trained deep K-tuplet network can extract discriminative features for unseen novel categories and can be seamlessly incorporated with a non-linear distance metric function to facilitate few-shot classification.
The proposed method's result on the miniImageNet benchmark outperforms other metric-based few-shot classification methods.

When evaluated on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars using the model trained with miniImageNet, the proposed method significantly outperforms prior methods, demonstrating superior capability to generalize to unseen classes.

The deep K-tuplet Network generalizes the triplet network to allow joint comparison with K negative samples in each mini-batch, making feature embedding learning more faithful to few-shot classification with improved feature generalization.
The semi-hard mining sampling technique is presented as an effective sampling strategy to sample informative hard triplets, which can speed up convergence and stabilize the training procedure.
The proposed technique can be seamlessly incorporated with the learnable non-linear distance metric for few-shot classification.

claim_records.text: The proposed Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The proposed ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The proposed loss functions show a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed methods demonstrate competitive generalization capabilities to other domains including Caltech, CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets compared with the state of the art.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The obtained accuracy results on Mini-Imagenet represent an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The ICNN Loss measures the intra and inter class distances of batch points and assigns each data point an Inter and Intra Class Nearest Neighbors score.
The Proto-Triplet Loss is based on triplet loss and calculates the similarity between points using prototypes of different classes as anchor, positive, and negative points.
Both the ICNN Loss and Proto-Triplet Loss aim to increase the inter-class distance and decrease the intra-class distance between samples of different classes.
The ICNN loss represents a novel loss function that evaluates the quality of the features obtained based on the inter/intra class, the variance and the class ratio from nearest neighbors.
Current deep learning algorithms tend to overfit when they are given a small dataset for training, limiting their generalization capabilities.

The main challenge for few-shot learning is to apply a fine-tuning process to an existing embedding network to adapt it to new classes, and such process can easily lead to overfitting due to the few labeled samples available for each class.
Metric-learning methods learn a pairwise similarity metric such that a score given by some distance is high for similar samples, whilst dissimilar samples get a low score.
Only a few methods have explored mechanisms for enforcing class separability via a custom loss function during training.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification classify unseen samples by their distances to few seen samples in a learned deep neural network embedding space, avoiding overfitting to few training images and achieving state-of-the-art performance.

This review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification published from 2018 to 2022 into three groups aligned with three metric learning stages: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of novel classes are classified by computing their distances to novel support images under the learned measure, followed by a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest neighbors.

fact_fields.method: Supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify query samples by measuring and comparing their distance to support samples, but scarce support samples have limited capacity to represent the novel class.

Class prototypes used in few-shot metric learning can be constructed as simple or weighted averages of feature embeddings, or learned end-to-end to improve representation ability; some works also use class distributions or subspaces as class representations.

Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure sample distances, and computes query class assignment confidence by estimating each class distribution via a neural network.

fact_fields.method: Variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning

claim_records.text: Simon et al. proposed the Deep Subspace Network (DSN), which represents each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition, and classifies queries by nearest subspace assignment based on Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class subspace.
The DSN method is reported to be more robust to noises and outliers than the Prototypical Network.
Few-shot classification aims to learn a classification rule from typically 1-5 labeled examples per class, and faces a high risk of model overfitting to the small number of labeled training samples.

Metric learning methods for few-shot classification learn feature embeddings and/or distance/similarity measures, classifying unseen samples based on distance to labeled samples or class representations, with same-class samples expected to be close in embedding space and different-class samples expected to be far apart.

Meta-learning methods for few-shot classification train a meta-learner across many different classification tasks to extract generalizable knowledge, enabling rapid learning on a new related task with few examples.

Transfer learning methods for few-shot classification assume shared knowledge between source and target domains, and fine-tune a model trained on abundant source data to fit few labeled target samples.

This review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification published from 2018 to 2022 into three groups aligned with three metric learning stages: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of novel classes are classified by computing their distances to novel support images under the learned measure, followed by a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest neighbors.

Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify query samples by measuring and comparing their distance to support samples, but scarce support samples have limited capacity to represent the novel class.

Class prototypes used in few-shot metric learning can be constructed as simple or weighted averages of feature embeddings, or learned end-to-end to improve representation ability; some works also use class distributions or subspaces as class representations.

Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure sample distances, and computes query class assignment confidence by estimating each class distribution via a neural network.

Simon et al. proposed the Deep Subspace Network (DSN), which represents each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition, and classifies queries by nearest subspace assignment based on Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class subspace.
The DSN method is reported to be more robust to noises and outliers than the Prototypical Network.
Few-shot classification aims to learn a classification rule from typically 1-5 labeled examples per class, and faces a high risk of model overfitting to the small number of labeled training samples.

Metric learning methods for few-shot classification learn feature embeddings and/or distance/similarity measures, classifying unseen samples based on distance to labeled samples or class representations, with same-class samples expected to be close in embedding space and different-class samples expected to be far apart.

Meta-learning methods for few-shot classification train a meta-learner across many different classification tasks to extract generalizable knowledge, enabling rapid learning on a new related task with few examples.

Transfer learning methods for few-shot classification assume shared knowledge between source and target domains, and fine-tune a model trained on abundant source data to fit few labeled target samples.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-support pair similarities and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.
UAFS converts observed query-support similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporates them into the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to jointly consider similarities between a query and prototypes in a support set and estimate the uncertainty of each query-prototype pair.

fact_fields.method: Graph-based model for similarity uncertainty estimation

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments show the proposed UAFS method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, UAFS takes each query-prototype pair as a node and employs a graph-based model to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each pair.

Rather than a scalar, UAFS models the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj by a distribution, referred to as probabilistic similarity, based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation.

fact_fields.method: Probabilistic similarity modeling with graph-based uncertainty estimation

claim_records.text: The UAFS network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses that exploit the estimated similarity uncertainty.

fact_fields.method: Uncertainty-aware optimization with similarity-based classification losses

claim_records.text: Few-shot image classification aims to classify query samples of new categories given only a few labeled support samples of these categories.

In similarity-based few-shot classification, the logit vector for a query sample is obtained by feeding similarities between the query and prototypes to a SoftMax function, making the reliability of estimated similarity vital to classification performance.
Aleatoric uncertainty captures noise inherent in observations and identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample.
For few-shot image classification, an observed query-prototype similarity suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.

In the proposed UAFS framework, the observed feature similarity between a query and a prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

claim_records.text: Existing metric-based few-shot classification algorithms often fail to generalize to unseen domains due to large discrepancy of feature distribution across domains.
The proposed method uses feature-wise transformation layers for augmenting image features using affine transforms to simulate various feature distributions under different domains during training.

fact_fields.method: Feature-wise transformation layers with affine transforms

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of feature distributions under different domains.
Experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models and provides consistent improvements on few-shot classification performance under domain shift.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method proposed for few-shot image classification that aims to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify specific mutually related regions in query and support images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
RCN's interpretability can be generalized from the task level to the category level, which can be viewed as a way to find prototypical parts supporting RCN's final decision.
Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets show RCN is effective over existing baselines for few-shot image classification.
RCN's final classification decision is directly linked to region similarities in the last layer, forming a simple and easily explained linear process compared to attention mechanisms.
RCN includes a region meta learner, a dynamic system designed to adapt to different meta tasks during both training and testing stages.
RCN learns a generated weight of regions to explain which regions in a support sample are similar to locations in a query sample and which of these regions the model prefers to compare.
RCN is designed to find which parts in a query sample are most similar to manually selected regions in a support sample by computing similarity between them.
RCN generates a region weight in its final stage to define which common parts between support and query samples most influence the final similarity score.
Few-shot learning methods are grouped into metric-based models and gradient-based models in the presented related work review.

claim_records.text: MF-Adapter (Meta-Feature Adaption method) combines complementary strengths of low-level local representations and high-level semantic representations for few-shot classification.
MF-Unit (Meta-Feature Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric designed to measure category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.

MF-Unit is obtained by inductive representation of local feature maps at different scales using sliding windows with different perceptual fields, containing rich local information representing category-consistent characteristics.

Before model training, support set images are encoded into different-level features by a fixed CLIP visual encoder, and low-level feature maps are unfolded into Meta-Feature using a list of sliding windows with different scales.
MF-Unit is calculated by applying inductive max and mean operations on each sliding window, and is regarded as category-consistent features containing inductive knowledge.

During inference, MF-Adapter first converts test images into MF-Units at different levels and scales, retrieves few-shot knowledge in the support set's MF-Unit space to get local logits, then combines this with the original CLIP high-level prediction for the final prediction.
MF-Adapter is the first work to utilize the local similarity of CLIP for few-shot learning, combining complementary strengths of low-level and high-level semantic representations.
Comprehensive experiments on 11 widely adopted datasets for few-shot classification show MF-Adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with previous CLIP-based methods.
Existing CLIP-based few-shot methods including CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features fully aligned with textual features representing the 'Summary' of images.
Low-level local representations (LRs) are more consistent between seen and unseen samples than high-level representations for few-shot classification.

In few-shot classification with insufficient seen images, the standard 'pre-training & fine-tuning' paradigm does not produce better results, so common practice is to fix CLIP pre-training weights and learn a lightweight module.
Tip-Adapter achieves large performance gains compared to both prompt-based methods and CLIP-Adapter on several classification datasets by fine-tuning a trainable query-key cache layer on top of CLIP.

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks are proposed for few-shot classification, where a classifier must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set given only a small number of examples of each new class.
Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classification is performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class.
Prototypical networks reflect a simpler inductive bias beneficial in the limited-data few-shot regime and achieve excellent results compared to recent few-shot learning approaches.
Analysis shows that some simple design decisions for prototypical networks can yield substantial improvements over recent approaches involving complicated architectural choices and meta-learning.
Prototypical networks extended to zero-shot learning achieve state-of-the-art results on the CU-Birds dataset.

claim_records.text: Some recent work shows that local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.

Existing local descriptor based few-shot learning works are still based on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure relations between query images and support classes.
Given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class, an asymmetric measure is argued to be more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning.
The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic in comparison to image classification.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes as input an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: The proposed QSFormer model integrates a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch to simultaneously model the two core challenges of few-shot classification.

The sampleFormer branch of QSFormer adopts Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model Support representation, Query image representation and metric learning for few-shot classification.

The local patch Transformer branch of QSFormer extracts structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches, serving as a complement to the global learning branch.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the QSFormer few-shot learning method.
All modules of QSFormer are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer.

HyperShot relies on relations between embeddings of support examples instead of direct feature values provided by backbone models.
HyperShot is claimed to be able to adapt to highly different tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks with the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
The STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
The STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During training, the STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.

Extensive experiments show the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

fact_fields.method: Siamese Transformer Network (STN) evaluated via extensive experiments

claim_records.text: Network intrusion detection systems face significant challenges in identifying emerging attack patterns, especially when limited data samples are available.

The proposed Multi-Space Prototypical Learning (MSPL) framework operates across multiple metric spaces—Euclidean, Cosine, Chebyshev, and Wasserstein distances—integrated through a constrained weighting scheme to enhance embedding robustness and improve pattern recognition.
The MSPL framework leverages Polyak-averaged prototype generation to stabilize the learning process and effectively adapt to rare and zero-day attacks.
The MSPL framework uses an episodic training paradigm to ensure balanced representation across diverse attack classes, enabling robust generalization.

Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSPL outperforms traditional approaches in detecting low-profile and novel attack types, establishing it as a robust solution for zero-day attack detection.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) obtains the relational map between supports and queries effectively for few-shot tasks.

FS-CT consists of two parts: a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.

Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, enhances the transformer module significantly and improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
FS-CT performs competitive results in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition is developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.
FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm that can be applied for a wide range of applications, such as healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed for cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two core steps: 1) Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and 2) Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The RMP step of HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, to support better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

The REP step of HelixFormer uses CSRMs to strengthen extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.
Experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks show HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The official code for HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics under low-data regimes.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless for classification due to limited receptive field.

DMN4 (Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network) is proposed for FSL, which establishes a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation to explicitly select query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters.

claim_records.text: FiT combines transfer learning (fixed pretrained backbones and fine-tuned FiLM adapter layers) and meta-learning (automatically configured Naive Bayes classifiers and episodic training) to produce parameter efficient models with superior low-shot image classification accuracy.
FiT achieves better classification accuracy than the leading Big Transfer (BiT) algorithm at low-shot across a wide range of downstream datasets.
FiT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the VTAB-1k benchmark using fewer than 1% of the updateable parameters.

FiT demonstrates parameter efficiency and superior accuracy in distributed low-shot applications including model personalization and federated learning where model update size is an important performance metric.
The parameter efficiency of FiT enables few-shot learning, inexpensive model updates for personalization, and communication efficient federated learning.

claim_records.text: In meta-learning for few-shot classification, the number of labeled examples per category used during meta-training impacts recognition performance at meta-test time.
Generally, the shot number used in meta-training should match the shot number used in meta-testing to obtain the best few-shot classification performance.
The paper introduces a theoretical analysis of the impact of shot number on Prototypical Networks, a state-of-the-art few-shot classification method.
The paper proposes a simple method that is robust to the choice of shot number used during meta-training, a crucial hyperparameter for few-shot learning.

claim_records.text: The introduced semi-supervised few-shot learning approach, Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN), is built on top of Prototypical Networks (PN).
The developed random walk semi-supervised loss enables the network to learn representations that are compact and well-separated.

Compact and well-separated class representations can be achieved by modeling the prototypical random walk notion without needing additional graph-NN parameters or a transductive setting where a collective test set is provided.
The PRWN model outperforms baselines in most benchmarks, with significant improvements in some cases.
PRWN trained with 40% of data as labeled compares competitively against fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% of labels.

claim_records.text: In the 1-shot mini-Imagenet case, PRWN trained with 40% labeled data achieves 50.89% accuracy, outperforming fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% labels which achieve 49.4% accuracy.
