claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks with the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized with pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
The STN applies Euclidean distance measure to global features and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
The STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
During training, the STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network.

Extensive experiments show the STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

fact_fields.method: Siamese Transformer Network (STN) evaluated via extensive experiments

claim_records.text: Existing few-shot image classification methods often emphasize either global features or local features, with few studies considering the integration of both.

fact_fields.method: observational analysis of existing few-shot image classification methods

claim_records.text: Network intrusion detection systems face significant challenges in identifying emerging attack patterns, especially when limited data samples are available.

The proposed Multi-Space Prototypical Learning (MSPL) framework operates across multiple metric spaces—Euclidean, Cosine, Chebyshev, and Wasserstein distances—integrated through a constrained weighting scheme to enhance embedding robustness and improve pattern recognition.
The MSPL framework leverages Polyak-averaged prototype generation to stabilize the learning process and effectively adapt to rare and zero-day attacks.
The MSPL framework uses an episodic training paradigm to ensure balanced representation across diverse attack classes, enabling robust generalization.

Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSPL outperforms traditional approaches in detecting low-profile and novel attack types, establishing it as a robust solution for zero-day attack detection.

claim_records.text: The proposed patch-driven relational refinement learns cache adapter weights from intra-image patch dependencies rather than treating an image embedding as a monolithic vector.

The introduced relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) obtains the relational map between supports and queries effectively for few-shot tasks.

FS-CT consists of two parts: a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.

Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, enhances the transformer module significantly and improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.
FS-CT performs competitive results in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition is developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.
FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm that can be applied for a wide range of applications, such as healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed for cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two core steps: 1) Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and 2) Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The RMP step of HelixFormer enables each branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, to support better cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

The REP step of HelixFormer uses CSRMs to strengthen extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle feature differences of fine-grained objects.
Experiments on five public fine-grained benchmarks show HelixFormer achieves much better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The official code for HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: In few-shot learning, the conventional pooled global feature is likely to lose useful local characteristics under low-data regimes.

Existing deep descriptor-based FSL methods generally take all deep descriptors from neural networks into consideration, ignoring that some descriptors are useless for classification due to limited receptive field.

DMN4 (Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network) is proposed for FSL, which establishes a Mutual Nearest Neighbor (MNN) relation to explicitly select query descriptors most relevant to each task and discard less relevant ones from aggregative clutters.

fact_fields.method: DMN4 (Discriminative Mutual Nearest Neighbor Neural Network)

claim_records.text: Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMN4 outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on both fine-grained and generalized datasets.

claim_records.text: Image background common in realistic images is empirically identified as a shortcut knowledge helpful for in-class classification but ungeneralizable beyond training categories in Few-Shot Learning.

Extensive experiments carried on inductive FSL tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the COSOC approach.

FiT achieves better classification accuracy than the leading Big Transfer (BiT) algorithm at low-shot across a wide range of downstream datasets.
FiT achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on the VTAB-1k benchmark using fewer than 1% of the updateable parameters.

FiT demonstrates parameter efficiency and superior accuracy in distributed low-shot applications including model personalization and federated learning where model update size is an important performance metric.
The parameter efficiency of FiT enables few-shot learning, inexpensive model updates for personalization, and communication efficient federated learning.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that BaseTransformers works well for several backbones and achieves state-of-the-art results in the inductive one shot setting.

claim_records.text: In meta-learning for few-shot classification, the number of labeled examples per category used during meta-training impacts recognition performance at meta-test time.
Generally, the shot number used in meta-training should match the shot number used in meta-testing to obtain the best few-shot classification performance.
The paper introduces a theoretical analysis of the impact of shot number on Prototypical Networks, a state-of-the-art few-shot classification method.
The paper proposes a simple method that is robust to the choice of shot number used during meta-training, a crucial hyperparameter for few-shot learning.

fact_fields.method: proposed simple method derived from theoretical analysis of Prototypical Networks

claim_records.text: The model trained for an arbitrary meta-training shot number shows strong performance across different values of meta-testing shot numbers.
The proposed approach is experimentally demonstrated on different few-shot classification benchmarks.

claim_records.text: The introduced semi-supervised few-shot learning approach, Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN), is built on top of Prototypical Networks (PN).
The developed random walk semi-supervised loss enables the network to learn representations that are compact and well-separated.

Compact and well-separated class representations can be achieved by modeling the prototypical random walk notion without needing additional graph-NN parameters or a transductive setting where a collective test set is provided.
The PRWN model outperforms baselines in most benchmarks, with significant improvements in some cases.
PRWN trained with 40% of data as labeled compares competitively against fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% of labels.

fact_fields.method: Prototypical Random Walk Networks (PRWN) vs fully supervised Prototypical Networks

claim_records.text: In the 1-shot mini-Imagenet case, PRWN trained with 40% labeled data achieves 50.89% accuracy, outperforming fully supervised Prototypical Networks trained on 100% labels which achieve 49.4% accuracy.

claim_records.text: Boundary patches corresponding to pixels located at the boundary of objects in hyperspectral images are hard to classify, as they are mixed with multi-class spectral information.
The proposed APNT method uses a transformer as feature extractor to learn pixel-to-pixel relations and apply different attentions to different pixels, with the prototype network as the backbone.

APNT randomly mixes up two hyperspectral image patches to imitate boundary patches, using these synthetic patches for training to enlarge the number of hard training samples and enhance their diversity.
APNT follows the TransMix data augmentation technique, using attention returned by the transformer to mix up labels of two patches to generate better labels for synthetic patches.
The proposed APNT method demonstrates state of the art performance and better robustness for few-shot hyperspectral image classification compared with existing methods in experiments.

Few-shot hyperspectral image classification aims to identify the class of each pixel using only a small number of labeled pixels, and fixed-size patches centered around each pixel are commonly used to obtain spatial-spectral joint features.
APNT does not directly use patches cut from hyperspectral images for training, instead using randomly mixed synthetic patches.

claim_records.text: Proto-CLIP is a few-shot learning framework that leverages large-scale vision-language models such as CLIP, utilizing both image prototypes and text prototypes for few-shot learning.

Proto-CLIP adapts image and text encoder embeddings from CLIP in a joint fashion using few-shot examples, and uses embeddings from the two encoders to compute respective image class prototypes for classification.

During adaptation, Proto-CLIP aligns image and text prototypes of corresponding classes, and this alignment is beneficial for few-shot classification due to reinforced contributions from both types of prototypes.
Proto-CLIP has both training-free and fine-tuned variants.
The effectiveness of Proto-CLIP is demonstrated via experiments on benchmark datasets for few-shot learning, as well as in real-world robot perception scenarios.
Proto-CLIP is motivated by unimodal prototypical networks for few-shot learning.

assertions.source_quote: Few-shot image classification asks a model to recognize new visual categories from only a small labeled support set, commonly one to five examples per class, and then assign query images to those categories. The central difficulty is that ordinary supervised fine-tuning can overfit when each novel class has so few examples; metric-learning methods instead learn an embedding and/or comparison rule so that same-class images are close and different-class images are separated. This review therefore compares approaches by the point at which they add metric structure: the feature embedding, the class representation built from support examples, and the distance or similarity function used for the query decision. assertions.source_quote: The canonical episodic formulation samples support and query examples from many training tasks, encouraging training to resemble the novel-task test setting. Early metric methods compare a query directly with support images, while prototype-based methods summarize each support class into a reference vector, and relation-style methods learn a nonlinear comparator rather than relying only on a fixed Euclidean or cosine distance. These choices are not mutually exclusive: a method may learn embeddings through episodic metric objectives, aggregate support features into prototypes or richer subspaces, and still use a learned comparison network at inference. assertions.source_quote: At the class-representation stage, methods differ in what the support set is turned into before a query is scored. Direct support comparison keeps individual labeled examples as references; prototypical methods summarize each class with a point, typically by averaging support embeddings; distributional methods model uncertainty or class density; and subspace methods represent a class with a low-dimensional subspace rather than a single vector. These representations have different noise sensitivity and data requirements: point prototypes are simple, whereas distribution or subspace models attempt to capture within-class variation from the same scarce support examples. assertions.source_quote: At the decision stage, the criterion is how similarity is computed. Fixed-metric methods use predefined relations such as Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, nearest-subspace projection, or an explicitly combined global/local score. Learned-metric methods train a comparator—such as a relation module, MLP ranking head, attention/region interaction module, or weighted subspace-distance mechanism—to map paired or set-level evidence into a class score. A learned comparator and a learned embedding are therefore distinct design choices: one changes how features are produced, while the other changes how query and support evidence is compared. assertions.source_quote: Direct support-comparison methods are the simplest metric-learning family in the pipeline: an embedding network maps each query and labeled support image into the same space, and prediction follows nearest-neighbor or attention-weighted similarity rather than a separately optimized novel-class classifier. Matching Networks instantiate this episodic compare-to-support strategy with an end-to-end trainable k-nearest-neighbor style decision over support embeddings. Their contribution is to make meta-training resemble the support/query test episode, but their applicability boundary is that the support examples themselves carry the class representation: scarce, noisy, or atypical support images can directly distort the decision unless the embedding or attention mechanism compensates. Siamese networks are related pairwise comparators, but a pairwise similarity head alone does not aggregate multi-shot support information in the way prototype and relation methods do. assertions.source_quote: Prototypical methods move metric structure from individual examples to a class representation. For each sampled episode, support embeddings belonging to one class are summarized by a prototype—canonically a mean vector—and a query is classified according to its distance to those class prototypes. The mechanism is efficient and naturally handles one or several support shots, but it imposes a point-mass assumption: within-class variation is compressed into one reference vector. assertions.source_quote: Relation Networks replace a predefined Euclidean or cosine comparator with a learned nonlinear distance metric. The embedding network produces query and support/prototype features, a relation module receives their combined representation, and a shallow learned network outputs a relation score for class assignment. The main contribution is to separate representation geometry from comparator flexibility: the model can learn an episode-specific-looking nonlinear match instead of assuming that raw Euclidean distance is optimal. Its boundary is that a learned comparator does not by itself guarantee a well-separated embedding space; it also adds parameters and episodic training dependence, so poor support statistics or domain shift can still affect the relation score. Deep K-tuplet is explicitly described as compatible with this learnable nonlinear distance, showing that embedding shaping and learned comparison can be combined. assertions.source_quote: Relation Networks replace a predefined Euclidean or cosine comparator with a learned nonlinear distance metric. The embedding network produces query and support/prototype features, a relation module receives their combined representation, and a shallow learned network outputs a relation score for class assignment. The main contribution is to separate representation geometry from comparator flexibility: the model can learn an episode-specific-looking nonlinear match instead of assuming that raw Euclidean distance is optimal. Its boundary is that a learned comparator does not by itself guarantee a well-separated embedding space; it also adds parameters and episodic training dependence, so poor support statistics or domain shift can still affect the relation score. Deep K-tuplet is explicitly described as compatible with this learnable nonlinear distance, showing that embedding shaping and learned comparison can be combined. assertions.source_quote: Deep K-tuplet Network targets the embedding stage rather than proposing another final classifier. It revisits triplet metric learning because the desired embedding should place similar samples near one another and dissimilar samples farther apart, but it argues that an ordinary triplet update sees only one negative whereas few-shot episodes require comparison against multiple query samples, often from several classes. The method therefore generalizes the triplet network to compare an anchor jointly with K negative samples in a mini-batch and uses semi-hard mining to select informative hard triplets. Its claimed contribution is faster, more stable convergence and a more discriminative, transferable feature embedding for unseen classes; after embedding learning, it can be paired with a nonlinear distance metric. The evidence claimed in the paper is strongest for the specific miniImageNet-trained setting and cross-domain tests to Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars; it should not be read as evidence that K negatives universally outperform all non-metric meta-learners under different backbones or protocols. assertions.source_quote: Proto-Triplet and ICNN losses are later embedding-geometry methods that explicitly optimize intra-class compactness and inter-class separation in few-shot latent space. Proto-Triplet adapts triplet loss to the episodic prototype setting by using prototypes of different classes as anchor, positive, and negative elements rather than treating the loss as an ordinary instance-level triplet objective. ICNN instead assigns each point inter-class and intra-class nearest-neighbor scores and evaluates embedding quality from batch-level distances, variance, and the class ratio among nearest neighbors. Their shared mechanism is to jointly train the embedding network with a loss that enforces separability before nearest-prototype classification; they differ in whether the constraint is triplet/prototype based or nearest-neighbor statistics based. The paper reports miniImageNet accuracies of 61.32% for 5-way 1-shot and 79.93% for 5-way 5-shot with Proto-Triplet, and 60.79% and 80.41% with ICNN, while also testing CUB, Caltech, Dogs, and Cars for cross-domain behavior. These numbers support the method only under that paper's experimental setup and should be compared later against methods with matched backbone, episode sampling, and augmentation. assertions.source_quote: Subspace and distributional class representations relax the single-prototype assumption. In Deep Subspace Networks, each class is represented by a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples through singular value decomposition; a query is assigned by a nearest-subspace rule, using the distance between the query and its projection onto each class-specific subspace. The review reports this approach as more robust than Prototypical Networks to noise and outliers, a plausible mechanism because a subspace can express some within-class variation instead of collapsing all support examples to one point. Subspace Representation Learning extends this direction by representing an image with a subspace in local CNN feature space, measuring image similarity with weighted subspace distance, and aggregating K-shot support information through prototypical or discriminative template subspaces. Its applicability boundary is that estimating a meaningful subspace needs sufficient support diversity and stable local features; with one shot or highly redundant examples, the richer representation may be underdetermined even though the framework is designed around K-shot aggregation. assertions.source_quote: Region Comparison Network is a learned comparator with an explicitly spatial mechanism. Rather than comparing only global image embeddings, RCN learns which regions in query and support images correspond to or support one another, and it uses those region-level comparisons to produce the few-shot decision. Its contribution is both predictive and interpretive: Region Activation Mapping visualizes intermediate comparison variables, and the method extends interpretation from an individual task toward category-level prototypical parts that explain the final decision. This differs from a generic relation module because the network's design and visualization are centered on local semantic correspondence rather than any learned nonlinear function over concatenated global features. Its boundary is that region correspondence is most useful when class identity is localized and shared across images; it adds interaction complexity and depends on CNN spatial features that may themselves fail under severe domain shift. assertions.source_quote: Region Comparison Network is a learned comparator with an explicitly spatial mechanism. Rather than comparing only global image embeddings, RCN learns which regions in query and support images correspond to or support one another, and it uses those region-level comparisons to produce the few-shot decision. Its contribution is both predictive and interpretive: Region Activation Mapping visualizes intermediate comparison variables, and the method extends interpretation from an individual task toward category-level prototypical parts that explain the final decision. This differs from a generic relation module because the network's design and visualization are centered on local semantic correspondence rather than any learned nonlinear function over concatenated global features. Its boundary is that region correspondence is most useful when class identity is localized and shared across images; it adds interaction complexity and depends on CNN spatial features that may themselves fail under severe domain shift. assertions.source_quote: RankDNN recasts few-shot recognition as relevance-ranking relation classification rather than conventional multiclass scoring. At meta-test time it ranks support images by their relevance to a query and assigns the query the label of its nearest support image. Its core comparator is a simple MLP that consumes an image triplet encoded through the difference of two vector-Kronecker products and predicts a binary relevance order. The method's contribution is a sample-efficient, domain-agnostic ranking relation that can be placed on top of different feature extractors and fused with post-processing methods. Because RankDNN is a ranking head rather than a fixed backbone, its evidence is conditional on the underlying extractor and fusion setup; the paper reports improvements across several backbones and benchmarks, but those results do not imply that the MLP ranking mechanism alone is independent of feature quality. [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58]

assertions.source_quote: Multi-stage embedding methods address a different limitation of traditional metric-based few-shot systems: relying on one distance between final query and support features can ignore shallow or intermediate visual information. MSENet uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces at different stages, applies self-attention to refine stage-wise representations, and learns stage weights so that global/abstract and earlier features can all contribute to the decision. Its mechanism therefore combines richer feature extraction with learned fusion rather than changing the task into ordinary supervised classification. The reported evaluation scope is 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot on MiniImageNet and FC100 plus cross-domain tests on eight benchmark datasets. Its boundary is that multiple outputs, attention, and learnable weights increase training and architectural complexity, and the method's claimed cross-domain advantage is tied to those tested target domains rather than establishing universal domain invariance. [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:e9dd9ee8e005]

assertions.source_quote: Global/local two-branch metric methods similarly challenge single-descriptor comparison, but through explicitly separate feature views. The Siamese Transformer Network uses two parallel Vision Transformer branches initialized from self-supervised pretraining: one branch supplies global features compared with Euclidean distance, while the other supplies local features compared with Kullback–Leibler divergence. The two metrics are L2-normalized and weighted into a final similarity score, and the whole network is fine-tuned with a meta-learning strategy. Its contribution is to combine complementary global category information and local detail without a separate complex feature-adaptation module. The method is not simply a fixed-distance prototype model: it depends on pretrained ViT branches, two non-identical metrics, and a learned weighting scheme. Its applicability is therefore strongest where self-supervised pretraining and transformer computation are available, and the reported superiority remains conditional on the four natural-image benchmarks and one-/five-shot protocols used in its study. [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45]

assertions.source_quote: ProtoTransfer is best understood as a transfer and initialization method that feeds a metric classifier, not as a new distance function. It constructs a metric embedding through self-supervised learning by clustering unlabeled prototypical samples with their augmentations, then uses that pretrained embedding as a starting point for few-shot classification by summarizing class clusters and fine-tuning. Its contribution is to reduce the annotation requirement of conventional supervised meta-learning while retaining prototype-style class summarization. The paper reports that it outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised meta-learning methods on miniImageNet few-shot tasks and, under domain shift, achieves comparable performance to supervised methods while using orders of magnitude fewer labels. Its boundary is important: comparisons to supervised methods are label-budget and domain-shift comparisons, and the method still relies on fine-tuning and unlabeled data availability; it should not be grouped with purely episodic supervised metric learners without noting that different supervision assumptions are involved. [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:124d7f0c2b82]

assertions.source_quote: Adaptive metric combination addresses task diversity rather than image geometry alone. The task-clustering approach from diverse few-shot learning first clusters tasks using matrix completion and then automatically selects a weighted combination of metrics learned from meta-training tasks for a newly encountered task. Its mechanism is relevant to metric learning because a single common similarity is treated as insufficient when tasks vary substantially, but the motivating evidence and experiments are natural-language sentiment and dialog-intent tasks rather than natural-image classification. It therefore serves as a conceptual contrast for image methods: adaptive metric mixtures may be useful when inter-task variance is high, but the cited result does not establish the same mechanism or performance for image episodes. It also should not be conflated with image methods that learn one nonlinear comparator end to end; the task-clustering method explicitly reasons over heterogeneous tasks and combines multiple task-derived metrics. assertions.source_quote: Multi-level relation learning for cross-domain hyperspectral images shows how metric methods can be specialized for a sensor domain. Existing metric-based hyperspectral approaches extract query and support features and predict from distance to support samples or prototypes, but the cited method argues that sample relations are underexploited. It retains a domain discriminator for domain-level distribution mismatch, adds contrastive learning for class-level relations and more discriminative features, and uses transformer cross-attention to model set-level relations from queries to support samples. Its contribution is therefore not merely another Euclidean prototype classifier: it combines domain alignment, embedding separation, and set-to-set attention. Its applicability boundary is the cross-domain hyperspectral setting; the sensor bands, spatial statistics, and source-target domain structure differ materially from natural-image benchmarks, so evidence from this method cannot be directly ranked against miniImageNet or CUB results without a shared protocol. [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b]

assertions.source_quote: Across these methods, the main mechanistic trade-off is representation richness versus estimability under scarcity. Nearest-support and simple prototype methods require little novel-task computation and make few assumptions beyond the learned embedding, but they are vulnerable to atypical support examples and point-representation collapse. Triplet, K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and ICNN losses improve the geometry of that embedding but require careful mining or batch statistics and do not remove the need for a final decision rule. Relation, region, ranking, attention, multi-stage, and global/local comparators increase decision flexibility and can exploit spatial or hierarchical evidence, but they introduce learned modules, pretraining dependencies, or multiple distances. Subspace and distributional representations model class variation more explicitly, yet they need enough support diversity to estimate the richer class model. assertions.source_quote: Domain-specific sensor benchmarks require their own tables. In FewSAR, 15 classic few-shot methods are implemented in three categories and evaluated under unified SAR protocols with both quantitative results and runtime; the benchmark authors observe that metric-learning methods attain the best accuracy, whereas meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, which they attribute primarily to bias in existing datasets. This is direct evidence only for the SAR benchmark and its included methods. assertions.source_quote: The first open problem is that metric learning does not remove the fundamental few-shot estimation risk: a support set with only one or a few examples can still produce an atypical embedding, prototype, subspace, or relation score. Direct nearest-support methods are exposed to individual noisy examples, while prototypes compress scarce support evidence into a point and can lose within-class variation. Richer distributional or subspace models can represent variation and are reported to be more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Networks in the Deep Subspace Network line, but they must estimate that structure from the same scarce support data; with one shot, redundant views, or unstable local features, the richer class model can be underdetermined rather than automatically more reliable. assertions.source_quote: A second problem is the trade-off between embedding-space constraints and the mining or batch statistics needed to make them work. Deep K-tuplet explicitly addresses the limitation of an ordinary triplet update seeing only one negative by jointly comparing K negatives and using semi-hard mining to find informative hard triplets; this is intended to stabilize and speed training, but it also makes results depend on negative composition and mining quality. Proto-Triplet and ICNN similarly enforce intra-class compactness and inter-class separation, yet ICNN relies on batch-level nearest-neighbor distances, variance, and class-ratio statistics. These objectives can improve geometry when episodes represent the test class structure, but poor sampling, too-easy negatives, overly hard negatives, or batch imbalance can weaken the learned embedding; the reported miniImageNet gains should not be interpreted as mining-free or universally stable improvements. Proto-Triplet and ICNN similarly enforce intra-class compactness and inter-class separation, yet ICNN relies on batch-level nearest-neighbor distances, variance, and class-ratio statistics. assertions.source_quote: Learned comparators create a separate bias–complexity problem. Relation Networks, region comparison modules, ranking MLPs, attention, and weighted multi-stage fusion can learn nonlinear matches that fixed Euclidean or cosine distances cannot express, but they add parameters and episodic training dependence. RCN shows the benefit of making comparisons spatial and interpretable through region correspondence and Region Activation Mapping, but that mechanism assumes discriminative information is localized and comparable across query and support images. RankDNN is deliberately backbone-agnostic and can improve different feature extractors, which also means its observed performance cannot be separated from the extractor and post-processing with which it is deployed. In general, a flexible comparator can fit episodic training tasks more closely while becoming more vulnerable when support statistics, image style, or target domain differ from meta-training. assertions.source_quote: Representation richness also brings architectural and pretraining dependencies. MSENet addresses the shallow-feature limitation of a single final-layer distance by using multiple stage outputs, self-attention refinement, and learnable stage weights; STN combines self-supervised ViT-Small global and local branches with Euclidean distance, KL divergence, normalization, and weighted fusion. These designs can capture complementary information, but they are not controlled tests of “more features always help”: the gains come as packages involving multiple outputs or branches, attention, learned weighting, transformer capacity, and self-supervised initialization. Their applicability therefore depends on compute, pretraining availability, and whether the target domain preserves the hierarchical or local/global regularities those features encode. assertions.source_quote: Cross-domain generalization remains a distinct and unresolved evaluation axis. Deep K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet/ICNN, RankDNN, and MSENet all report cross-dataset or cross-domain tests on collections such as CUB, Caltech, Dogs, Cars, or eight benchmark domains, and these results support transfer under their respective protocols. However, source training sets, target versions, backbones, and supervision assumptions are not shown in the selected evidence to be matched across papers. A model that separates classes well on miniImageNet may still fail when sensor statistics, backgrounds, object pose, granularity, or label semantics change; therefore cross-domain success in one target suite is evidence about that suite, not proof of domain-invariant metric learning. assertions.source_quote: Domain-specific imagery makes this limitation especially concrete. The FewSAR benchmark finds that, under its unified SAR protocols, metric-learning methods achieve the best accuracy while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, with the authors attributing the latter pattern largely to existing dataset bias. The hyperspectral multi-level relation method instead needs a domain discriminator, contrastive class relations, and transformer cross-attention to handle source–target mismatch. These findings show that no single natural-image metric design is automatically the right inductive bias for SAR or hyperspectral data: band structure, imaging physics, class granularity, background clutter, and available source labels can change both the best representation and the best comparator. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:30ce48d809b4] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b]

assertions.source_quote: Supervision assumptions complicate both method choice and reported progress. ProtoTransfer shows that self-supervised prototype-style transfer can outperform unsupervised meta-learning on miniImageNet and can be comparable to supervised methods under domain shift while using orders of magnitude fewer labels, but it still requires unlabeled data and fine-tuning. That result answers a label-budget question rather than showing parity under identical supervision with fully supervised episodic metric learners. Conversely, the strong transductive cross-entropy fine-tuning baseline is reported to outperform current methods on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 with the same hyperparameters. Its success is a benchmark-protocol warning: metric methods should be compared against carefully matched transfer and fine-tuning baselines, not only against other metric learners. assertions.source_quote: Benchmark and episode heterogeneity is itself an open problem because superiority claims are often protocol-conditional. The available studies report 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot results on common datasets, but the selected excerpts do not provide a common backbone, training schedule, augmentation, transductiveness setting, episode count, confidence interval, or runtime across methods. Exact Proto-Triplet and ICNN scores can be compared within their own paper, and FewSAR explicitly compares accuracy and runtime under one SAR benchmark, but many other claims are limited to each paper's selected baselines. Consequently, aggregate leaderboard ordering is unreliable unless those variables are matched; the fine-tuning study's proposal to quantify episode hardness further indicates that average accuracy alone may conceal task difficulty. assertions.source_quote: Interpretability is uneven across the pipeline. RCN is distinctive because it learns region-level comparisons and provides Region Activation Mapping plus category-level prototypical-part explanations, making some query–support evidence inspectable. Most other approaches discussed here expose less decision information: a Euclidean prototype distance says which prototype is nearest but not necessarily which visual evidence caused it; a learned relation score, weighted stage fusion, global/local weighting, or cross-attention map may be expressive but is not automatically a faithful explanation. Thus, even when a learned comparator improves accuracy, users in high-stakes settings still need validated visualization or attribution before treating the decision as interpretable. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Subspace and distributional class representations relax the single-prototype assumption. In Deep Subspace Networks, each class is represented by a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples through singular value decomposition; a query is assigned by a nearest-subspace rule, using the distance between the query and its projection onto each class-specific subspace. The review reports this approach as more robust than Prototypical Networks to noise and outliers, a plausible mechanism because a subspace can express some within-class variation instead of collapsing all support examples to one point. Subspace Representation Learning extends this direction by representing an image with a subspace in local CNN feature space, measuring image similarity with weighted subspace distance, and aggregating K-shot support information through prototypical or discriminative template subspaces. Its applicability boundary is that estimating a meaningful subspace needs sufficient support diversity and stable local features; with one shot or highly redundant examples, the richer representation may be underdetermined even though the framework is designed around K-shot aggregation. unsupported_claims.source_quote: The first open problem is that metric learning does not remove the fundamental few-shot estimation risk: a support set with only one or a few examples can still produce an atypical embedding, prototype, subspace, or relation score. Direct nearest-support methods are exposed to individual noisy examples, while prototypes compress scarce support evidence into a point and can lose within-class variation. Richer distributional or subspace models can represent variation and are reported to be more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Networks in the Deep Subspace Network line, but they must estimate that structure from the same scarce support data; with one shot, redundant views, or unstable local features, the richer class model can be underdetermined rather than automatically more reliable. unsupported_claims.source_quote: A second problem is the trade-off between embedding-space constraints and the mining or batch statistics needed to make them work. Deep K-tuplet explicitly addresses the limitation of an ordinary triplet update seeing only one negative by jointly comparing K negatives and using semi-hard mining to find informative hard triplets; this is intended to stabilize and speed training, but it also makes results depend on negative composition and mining quality. Proto-Triplet and ICNN similarly enforce intra-class compactness and inter-class separation, yet ICNN relies on batch-level nearest-neighbor distances, variance, and class-ratio statistics. These objectives can improve geometry when episodes represent the test class structure, but poor sampling, too-easy negatives, overly hard negatives, or batch imbalance can weaken the learned embedding; the reported miniImageNet gains should not be interpreted as mining-free or universally stable improvements. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Learned comparators create a separate bias–complexity problem. Relation Networks, region comparison modules, ranking MLPs, attention, and weighted multi-stage fusion can learn nonlinear matches that fixed Euclidean or cosine distances cannot express, but they add parameters and episodic training dependence. RCN shows the benefit of making comparisons spatial and interpretable through region correspondence and Region Activation Mapping, but that mechanism assumes discriminative information is localized and comparable across query and support images. RankDNN is deliberately backbone-agnostic and can improve different feature extractors, which also means its observed performance cannot be separated from the extractor and post-processing with which it is deployed. In general, a flexible comparator can fit episodic training tasks more closely while becoming more vulnerable when support statistics, image style, or target domain differ from meta-training. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Representation richness also brings architectural and pretraining dependencies. MSENet addresses the shallow-feature limitation of a single final-layer distance by using multiple stage outputs, self-attention refinement, and learnable stage weights; STN combines self-supervised ViT-Small global and local branches with Euclidean distance, KL divergence, normalization, and weighted fusion. These designs can capture complementary information, but they are not controlled tests of “more features always help”: the gains come as packages involving multiple outputs or branches, attention, learned weighting, transformer capacity, and self-supervised initialization. Their applicability therefore depends on compute, pretraining availability, and whether the target domain preserves the hierarchical or local/global regularities those features encode. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Cross-domain generalization remains a distinct and unresolved evaluation axis. Deep K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet/ICNN, RankDNN, and MSENet all report cross-dataset or cross-domain tests on collections such as CUB, Caltech, Dogs, Cars, or eight benchmark domains, and these results support transfer under their respective protocols. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Supervision assumptions complicate both method choice and reported progress. ProtoTransfer shows that self-supervised prototype-style transfer can outperform unsupervised meta-learning on miniImageNet and can be comparable to supervised methods under domain shift while using orders of magnitude fewer labels, but it still requires unlabeled data and fine-tuning. That result answers a label-budget question rather than showing parity under identical supervision with fully supervised episodic metric learners. Conversely, the strong transductive cross-entropy fine-tuning baseline is reported to outperform current methods on Mini-ImageNet, Tiered-ImageNet, CIFAR-FS, and FC-100 with the same hyperparameters. Its success is a benchmark-protocol warning: metric methods should be compared against carefully matched transfer and fine-tuning baselines, not only against other metric learners. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Interpretability is uneven across the pipeline. RCN is distinctive because it learns region-level comparisons and provides Region Activation Mapping plus category-level prototypical-part explanations, making some query–support evidence inspectable. Most other approaches discussed here expose less decision information: a Euclidean prototype distance says which prototype is nearest but not necessarily which visual evidence caused it; a learned relation score, weighted stage fusion, global/local weighting, or cross-attention map may be expressive but is not automatically a faithful explanation. Thus, even when a learned comparator improves accuracy, users in high-stakes settings still need validated visualization or attribution before treating the decision as interpretable. unsupported_claims.source_quote: Finally, the field lacks a single metric-learning solution that simultaneously dominates scarcity, within-class variation, domain shift, interpretability, label efficiency, and computational cost. Simple support or prototype comparisons are economical but make strong representation assumptions; embedding losses improve separation but depend on sampling; subspaces and distributions model variation but need support diversity; relation, region, ranking, attention, and multi-stage modules add flexibility and sometimes explanations but increase complexity; self-supervised and transformer methods introduce data and pretraining requirements. The practical implication is to select and evaluate methods under the target deployment conditions—way/shot, domain shift, sensor type, label budget, transductiveness, backbone, runtime, and need for explanations—rather than inferring a universal winner from unmatched benchmark averages. input.query: Compare metric-learning approaches for few-shot image classification.
input.survey:
# Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: An Embedding-to-Decision Comparison

## Abstract

This review compares metric-learning methods for few-shot image classification using a pipeline-based grouping: where metric structure is introduced—feature embedding, support-class representation, or query-to-class decision. Direct nearest-support and prototype methods offer simple references, while triplet/K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet and ICNN losses shape embedding geometry; relation, region, ranking, multi-stage and global/local comparators add learned matching flexibility; subspace and distributional models represent within-class variation more richly. The central trade-off is representation and decision richness against estimability, mining, architecture, pretraining and support-diversity requirements. Evidence is protocol-specific: the only cross-method numerical comparison available in the supplied excerpts is within the Proto-Triplet/ICNN study, where Mini-ImageNet 5-way accuracy is 61.32% versus 60.79% at 1 shot and 79.93% versus 80.41% at 5 shots. Other reported gains remain tied to each paper's dataset, backbone, way/shot episode, supervision and domain. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:8f2d3aeed0e0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:16194f2dc624] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:fef0a0efd75f] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:af582e4e661c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:cfe8011f36d7] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:508afe07fba7] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:c9a16c8b4307] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:83140db1cc86] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:4:fc29f7338649:claim:982b41a3ea6f] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:10e3a8ec7066] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:2:734f6afe7b8f:claim:104f2c92d98f] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:19a19b550bc8] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:3194b68af4ef] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:109e350ee013] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:38498384e907] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a195d65d3a29] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:c8bbee298669] [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:e9dd9ee8e005] [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:124d7f0c2b82]

Cross-domain, self-supervised and sensor-specific studies answer different questions rather than forming one leaderboard. Deep K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet/ICNN, RankDNN and MSENet report transfer tests, but their source and target protocols are not shown to be matched; ProtoTransfer addresses label efficiency through self-supervised prototype-style initialization; FewSAR and hyperspectral studies require separate evaluation because sensor data and domain-shift structure differ from natural-image benchmarks. Thus the review supports family-level mechanistic comparison and within-paper findings, but not a universal ranking or claim that any comparator, subspace, transformer or multi-metric design is generally best. [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:124d7f0c2b82] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:abstract:claim:4e73f8e2a349] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:abstract:claim:fc1acaacf362] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:section:1_introduction:0:44bf2e87d909:claim:dd1783ff2e5c] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:section:3_methodology:0:8abaf801d66d:claim:7f06c970f946] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:8f2d3aeed0e0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:508afe07fba7] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:30ce48d809b4] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:cfe8011f36d7] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:c9a16c8b4307] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:83140db1cc86] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:4:fc29f7338649:claim:982b41a3ea6f] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:e9dd9ee8e005] [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58] [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:097e69f218ad] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:417553186fa2] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:19a19b550bc8] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a195d65d3a29] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0] [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45]

## Introduction

Few-shot image classification asks a model to recognize new visual categories from only a small labeled support set, commonly one to five examples per class, and then assign query images to those categories. The central difficulty is that ordinary supervised fine-tuning can overfit when each novel class has so few examples; metric-learning methods instead learn an embedding and/or comparison rule so that same-class images are close and different-class images are separated. This review therefore compares approaches by the point at which they add metric structure: the feature embedding, the class representation built from support examples, and the distance or similarity function used for the query decision. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:417553186fa2] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:8f2d3aeed0e0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062] The canonical episodic formulation samples support and query examples from many training tasks, encouraging training to resemble the novel-task test setting. Early metric methods compare a query directly with support images, while prototype-based methods summarize each support class into a reference vector, and relation-style methods learn a nonlinear comparator rather than relying only on a fixed Euclidean or cosine distance. These choices are not mutually exclusive: a method may learn embeddings through episodic metric objectives, aggregate support features into prototypes or richer subspaces, and still use a learned comparison network at inference. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:16194f2dc624] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:fef0a0efd75f] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062] The scope here is image classification under few-shot episodes, including standard benchmarks such as miniImageNet and related cross-domain image tests, but not zero-shot recognition or NLP few-shot classification merely because they also use metric objectives. Closely related optimization-based meta-learning and transfer/fine-tuning baselines are treated as comparison points rather than members of the metric family. Domain-specific image settings such as SAR or hyperspectral classification are also distinguished from natural-image benchmarks because their sensors, class distributions, and evaluation protocols can change which method performs best. [E:arxiv:1607.08085:abstract:claim:a3268b9380ab] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:section:1_introduction:0:44bf2e87d909:claim:dd1783ff2e5c] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:30ce48d809b4] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b] The comparison will emphasize four questions. First, what representation does each method compare: individual support vectors, averaged prototypes, distributions, subspaces, regions, or multi-stage features? Second, what training objective shapes that representation: episodic nearest-neighbor/prototype loss, triplet or K-tuplet constraints, intra-/inter-class separation, ranking relations, or self-supervised transfer? Third, what is measured at test time: a fixed distance, a learned relation score, subspace distance, attention-weighted region match, or multi-metric combination? Finally, evidence is kept tied to its dataset, way/shot setting, backbone, baseline and domain; results from unmatched protocols are described as non-comparable rather than merged into a single ranking. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:8f2d3aeed0e0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:cfe8011f36d7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:83140db1cc86] [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a195d65d3a29] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:109e350ee013] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

This review uses a pipeline-based organizing choice—where metric structure is introduced in the few-shot decision—rather than treating all metric learners as one undifferentiated family. The three comparison stages are: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance or similarity measures. That grouping follows the review taxonomy used to organize deep metric-learning methods for few-shot image classification; it is an analytical lens for this comparison, not a claim that every paper uses the same labels or that methods must belong to only one stage. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:8f2d3aeed0e0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062]

At the embedding stage, the central criterion is whether the network is trained only to produce generic features or is explicitly shaped so that same-class samples are compact and different-class samples are separated. Triplet, K-tuplet, prototype-triplet, nearest-neighbor and contrastive objectives belong here because they constrain geometry in latent space before a final nearest-prototype or nearest-neighbor decision. Multi-stage networks also affect this stage when they produce features at different network depths and combine those feature spaces; region-based networks affect the comparison when they learn corresponding regions between query and support images. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:cfe8011f36d7] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:83140db1cc86] [E:arxiv:2311.01212:abstract:claim:bb0a20aa035b] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:3ed84c7988f0] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a195d65d3a29] [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45]

At the class-representation stage, methods differ in what the support set is turned into before a query is scored. Direct support comparison keeps individual labeled examples as references; prototypical methods summarize each class with a point, typically by averaging support embeddings; distributional methods model uncertainty or class density; and subspace methods represent a class with a low-dimensional subspace rather than a single vector. These representations have different noise sensitivity and data requirements: point prototypes are simple, whereas distribution or subspace models attempt to capture within-class variation from the same scarce support examples. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:05ec94865062] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:3194b68af4ef] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:19a19b550bc8]

At the decision stage, the criterion is how similarity is computed. Fixed-metric methods use predefined relations such as Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, nearest-subspace projection, or an explicitly combined global/local score. Learned-metric methods train a comparator—such as a relation module, MLP ranking head, attention/region interaction module, or weighted subspace-distance mechanism—to map paired or set-level evidence into a class score. A learned comparator and a learned embedding are therefore distinct design choices: one changes how features are produced, while the other changes how query and support evidence is compared. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:16194f2dc624] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:fef0a0efd75f] [E:arxiv:2211.15320:abstract:claim:51852c513b58] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:a195d65d3a29] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:38498384e907] [E:arxiv:2408.01427:abstract:claim:d6ca67f5ba45]

The taxonomy also separates training policy from metric architecture. Episodic meta-learning is a task-sampling and optimization setup in which support and query sets mimic test tasks; it can train embedding losses, prototypes, relation networks, ranking heads, or transformer comparators. Transfer learning and self-supervised pretraining are different sources of initialization or adaptation, not themselves equivalent to a distance function. Likewise, fine-tuning a cross-entropy classifier is an important baseline, but it should not be classified as metric learning unless its prediction rule actually compares query and support representations in learned feature space. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:417553186fa2] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:section:unknown:2:734f6afe7b8f:claim:104f2c92d98f] [E:arxiv:2006.11325:abstract:claim:124d7f0c2b82] [E:arxiv:1909.02729:abstract:claim:097e69f218ad] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:16194f2dc624]

Task and domain boundaries must be kept separate from these architectural stages. Few-shot image classification is distinct from zero-shot attribute prediction, where test classes are described by semantic attributes rather than represented by labeled support images. Natural-language few-shot tasks and adaptive combinations of text-task metrics do not directly establish image-method categories. SAR, hyperspectral, and other sensor-specific image benchmarks are image classification settings, but their domain shift and data distributions can alter method comparisons; they should be reported under their own protocols rather than merged with natural-image miniImageNet or tieredImageNet results.
